rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-ashudd denotes full strength, reason, and discernment; it is a plural form without a singular, like other collective plurals.
rows.anchor: الأشد كمال القوة والعقل والتمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation derives al-ashudd as a plural of shiddah, as an'am is a plural of ni'mah.
rows.anchor: وإن من الناس من قال إنه جمع شدة كأنعم جمع نعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading makes yatwaffa active, meaning that God completes the person's term; the majority read it passive, after strength and before decrepit old age.
rows.anchor: وقرىء يتوفى بفتح الياء أي يستوفي أجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Decrepit age brings bodily weakness and impaired reason, but has no fixed onset: some centenarians remain vigorous while younger adults weaken.
rows.anchor: ولا زمان لذلك محدود بل ذلك بحسب ما يقع في الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can bring a person from completed maturity to senility just as He developed him gradually, and can likewise resurrect bodies after their stages of development.
rows.anchor: فكذلك هو قادر على إعادة الأجساد التي درجها في هذه المناقل وإنشائها النشأة الثانية

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The purpose of the return to the weakest age is that a person can no longer understand anything after his former understanding.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي لكيلا يعقل من بعد عقله الأول شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the person can no longer acquire knowledge and forgets what he had learned.
rows.anchor: وقيل لكيلا يستفيد علما وينسى ما علمه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Old age can make new learning vanish almost immediately, so the person repeatedly asks who someone is just after being told.
rows.anchor: أي ليصير نساء بحيث إذا كسب علما في شيء لم ينشب أن ينساه

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ونافع
rows.claim: Abu Amr and Nafi are reported to give the mīm in al-umur a sukūn.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي عمرو ونافع تسكين ميم العمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's first proof of resurrection is human creation; unlike the earth's revival, not every stage of this proof can be directly seen.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الدليل الأول بعض مراتب الخلقة فيه غير مرتبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revived earth is a second proof visible to the eye, which is why the verse explicitly says that the listener sees it.
rows.anchor: ولما كان هذا الدليل الثاني مشاهدا للأبصار أحال ذلك على الرؤية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rain includes rainwater, rivers, springs, and irrigation; the earth's movement is loosened, shifting soil as plants emerge, and rabat means it swelled.
rows.anchor: والماء ماء المطر والأنهار والعيون والسواني واهتزازها تخلخلها واضطراب بعض أجسامها لأجل خروج النبات وربت أي زادت وانتفخت

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وعبد الله بن جعفر وخالد بن إلياس وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: These readers pronounce rabat with hamza, rabat, meaning it rose or stood high; Ibn Atiyya explains the earth as stretching upward with water like a lookout rising above ground.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وعبد الله بن جعفر وخالد بن إلياس وأبو عمرو في رواية وربأت بالهمز هنا وفي فصلت أي ارتفعت وأشرفت

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses rabi'an for a scout sent ahead, supporting the sense of rising to a high lookout.
rows.anchor: بعثنا ربيئا قبل ذلك مخملا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Creator who brought about human development and revived earth truly exists and can revive the dead; since He promised resurrection and can do it, it must occur.
rows.anchor: وهو حقيقته تعالى فه الثابت الموجود القادر على إحياء الموتى وعلى كل مقدور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that the Hour is coming reinforces that God revives the dead; it is apparently an independent assertion, not part of the preceding causal clause.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله وأن الساعة آتية ليس داخلا في سبب ما تقدم ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative parses the demonstrative as an object governed by an omitted verb, meaning that God did this.
rows.anchor: وقيل ذلك منصوب بمضمر أي فعلنا ذلك

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b identifies the person disputing about God without knowledge as al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.
rows.anchor: فعن محمد بن كعب أنها نزلت في الأخنس بن شريق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the disputant as Abu Jahl.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس في أبي جهل

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify both disputant passages as concerning al-Nadr, repeated for stronger condemnation and because each passage adds a point absent from the other; more than ten verses were reportedly revealed about him.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أنها والتي قبلها في النضر كررت مبالغة في الذم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reads the second passage's conjunction as reproachful repetition: despite clear proofs, some still dispute; he distinguishes it from the earlier conjunction linking statements.
rows.anchor: وكرر هذه على وجه التوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction in the second passage is not circumstantial: it divides the condemned into disputants and those who worship God precariously, while knowledge means necessary knowledge, guidance means reasoning, and the clear Book means revelation.
rows.anchor: وإنما هي للعطف قسم المخذولين إلى مجادل في الله بغير علم متبع لشيطان مريد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains thaniya 'itf as haughtiness; Mujahid says the person turns his neck contemptuously, and al-Dahhak says he raises his nose arrogantly.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: متكبرا، ومجاهد: لاويا عنقه

rows.speaker: ابن جريج ومجاهد وأهل مكة وأبو عمرو
rows.claim: A reading with an open yā in li-yuḍilla means the disputant misleads himself; the majority's ḍamma reading means he misleads others, increasing his burden through their deeds.
rows.anchor: ليضل بفتح الياء أي ليضل في نفسه والجمهور بضمها أي ليضل غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because his argument leads to misguidance and he turns away from guidance toward false argument, he is portrayed as moving from guidance into error.
rows.anchor: ولما كان مآل جداله إلى الإضلال كان كأنه علة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worldly disgrace refers to capture, killing, and defeat at Badr; al-Nadr was captured, with a report locating this at al-Safra'.
rows.anchor: والخزي في الدنيا ما لحقه يوم بدر من الأسر والقتل والهزيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hariq may be a level of Hell, or a descriptive genitive meaning the burning punishment.
rows.anchor: والحريق قيل طبقة من طباق جهنم

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads fa-udhīqahu with a first-person hamza: 'so I make him taste.'
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي فأذيقه بهمزة المتكلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative's syntax follows the same possible parses already discussed for the earlier demonstrative in 'that is because God is the Real.'
rows.anchor: وجوزوا في إعراب ذلك هذا ما جوزوا في إعراب ذلك بأن الله هو الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What one's hands sent ahead means the person's wrongdoing, while the sentence also points to God's justice in punishing disobedience; the clause about God may begin a new assertion.
rows.anchor: أي باجترامك وبعدل الله فيك إذ عصيته

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says 'servants' here highlights their helplessness and limited power, a distinction Abū Hayyan had challenged in his discussion of Āl ʿImrān.
rows.anchor: والعبيد هنا ذكروا في معنى مسكنتهم وقلة قدرتهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وغيرهم
rows.claim: The verse is said to concern converts among Bedouins who feared Muhammad would not prevail and that their Jewish allies would then stop hosting and protecting them.
rows.anchor: من يعبد الله نزلت في أعراب من أسلم وغطفان تباطؤوا عن الإسلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وغيرهم
rows.claim: Another report concerns uncertain converts who prospered in wealth or sons and called Islam good, but reverted in adversity, as the Uraniyyin did.
rows.anchor: في أعراب لا يقين لهم يسلم أحدهم فيتفق تثمير ماله وولادة ذكر وغير ذلك من الخير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also identifies the person as Shayba ibn Rabi'a, who embraced Islam before the Prophet's mission and apostatized after revelation began.
rows.anchor: في شيبة بن ربيعة أسلم قبل ظهور الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says a Jewish convert, stricken by misfortune, became pessimistic about Islam and asked the Prophet to undo his conversion; the verse was then revealed.
rows.anchor: في يهودي أسلم فأصيب فتشاءم بالإسلام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the verse describes a hypocrite who worships with his tongue but not his heart.
rows.anchor: هو المنافق يعبده بلسانه دون قلبه

rows.speaker: ابن عيسى
rows.claim: Ibn Isa explains the precarious worship as arising from weak conviction.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عيسى: على ضعف يقين

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd glosses 'upon an edge' as being in doubt.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيد على حرف على شك

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya explains 'upon an edge' as deviating from clear doctrine or standing on its brink, ready to fall away.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية حرف على انحراف منه عن العقيدة البيضاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari pictures the worshipper as on the edge rather than the center of religion: secure if victory and spoils come, but ready to flee if not.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري على حرف على طرف من الدين لا في وسطه وقلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly loss is suffering loss of property or loved ones without accepting God's decree; afterlife loss is forfeiting the reward of patience by apostatizing.
rows.anchor: وخسرانه الدنيا إصابته فيها بما يسوؤه من ذهاب ماله وفقد أحبائه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وحميد والأعرج وابن محيصن وقنب والجحدري وابن مقسم
rows.claim: These readers pronounce khāsir al-dunyā as an accusative active participle functioning as a circumstantial expression.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وحميد والأعرج وابن محيصن من طريق الزعفراني وقعنب والجحدري وابن مقسم خاسر الدنيا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A nominative active-participle reading can make 'loser' the subject, replacing the pronoun with an explicit noun; al-Zamakhshari regards this as a good parse.
rows.anchor: والرفع على الفاعلية ووضع الظاهر موضع الضمير

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read khasira as a past-tense verb, either a fresh report or a circumstantial clause without qad; Abu al-Fadl also permits it as a substitute for 'turned back.'
rows.anchor: خسر فعلا ماضيا وهو استئناف إخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial of harm and benefit concerns idols, while the nearer harm than benefit concerns intelligent claimants to divinity, such as Pharaoh and the Maghribi Banu Ubayd rulers in Egypt; any worldly benefit is outweighed by enslavement and eternal punishment.
rows.anchor: وذلك لاختلاف المتعلق، وذلك أن قوله ما لا ينفعه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari resolves the apparent contradiction by taking the first clause as God's account of powerless idols and the second as idolaters' future cry: they suffer harm from worship and get no intercession.
rows.anchor: والجملة الثانية من كلام عباد الأصنام يقولون ذلك في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects this solution because an idol cannot have any benefit at all, so its harm cannot meaningfully be compared with a benefit.
rows.anchor: والذي أقول إن الصنم ليس له نفع ألبتة حتى يقال ضره أقرب من نفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reconciliation says idols do not themselves harm or benefit, but their worship causes harm, just as idols are called misleading because they occasion misguidance.
rows.anchor: بأنها لا تضر ولا تنفع بأنفسها ولكن عبادتها نسب الضرر إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reconciliation reads the second assertion concessively: although idols truly do not harm or benefit, even if they did, their harm would exceed their benefit.
rows.anchor: هي في الحقيقة لا تضر ولا تنفع بين ذلك في الآية الأولى ثم أثبت لها الضر والنفع في الثانية على طريق التسليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians offer several parses for the repeated yadu'u, including verbal emphasis with no object and a construction where the demonstrative is its object.
rows.anchor: فقالوا يدعوا إما أن يكون لها تعلق بقوله لمن ضره أولا إن لم يكن لها تعلق

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: One parse makes 'that' the object of yadu'u and treats the demonstrative as a relative pronoun, a usage available only to Kufans and only after an interrogative particle.
rows.anchor: وجعل موصولا بمعنى الذي قاله أبو علي الفارسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial parse that estimates a passive participle is weak: active yadu'uhu yields dāʿiyan, not madʿūwan; passive yudʿā would fit the latter.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف، لأن يدعوه لا يقدر مدعوا إنما يقدر داعيا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash takes yadu'u to mean 'says,' with the following relative clause as subject and an omitted predicate meaning a god; the proposal is criticized because idolaters never believed harm exceeded benefit.
rows.anchor: ما قاله الأخفش وهو أن يدعوا بمعنى يقول ولمن مبتدأ موصول صلته الجملة بعده

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: On al-Akhfash's parse, the closing 'how evil a protector' must start a new sentence because idolaters would not describe their idols that way.
rows.anchor: في هذا القول يكون لبئس مستأنفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second parse takes yadu'u as 'names' with an omitted second object meaning god, but it requires an extra lam in the text.
rows.anchor: أن يدعوا بمعنى يسمي

rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: The stronger analysis treats prayer like a verb of belief and supplies the sense 'claims'; the relative clause is its object and 'for whom' its predicate.
rows.anchor: والأحسن أن يضمن معنى يزعم ويقدر لمن خبره

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra' says the lam is displaced, yielding 'he calls upon one whose harm is nearer than benefit'; Abū Hayyan objects that a relative clause cannot precede its antecedent.
rows.anchor: ما قاله الفراء وهو أن اللام دخلت في غير موضعها والتقدير يدعوا من لضره أقرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis calls the lam emphatic and takes 'whom' as the object, but the lam is not normally extra in this construction; the reading without it lends support.
rows.anchor: لكن يقويه قراءة عبد الله يدعو من ضره بإسقاط اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closest analysis makes the second yadu'u an emphatic repetition of the first, takes the lam as initial, and supplies an oath whose answer is 'how evil a protector.'
rows.anchor: وأقرب التوجيهات أن يكون يدعوا توكيدا ليدعو الأول واللام في لمن لام الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here yadu'u apparently means calling out for help; al-mawla means helper and al-ashir means intimate companion.
rows.anchor: والمولى هنا الناصر والعشير الصاحب المخالط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing the insecurity and loss of those who worship precariously, the passage contrasts them with believers' promised reward and then rebukes doubters of the Prophet's victory.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى حالة من يعبده على حرف وسفه رأيه وتوعده بخسرانه في الآخرة عقبه بذكر حال مخالفيهم من أهل الإيمان

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets the challenge as a proverbial 'take the rope and hang yourself' taunt toward someone seeking the impossible.
rows.anchor: على جهة المثل السائر قولهم: دونك الحبل فاختنق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والكلبي ومقاتل والضحاك وقتادة وابن زيد والسدي
rows.claim: These authorities understand the pronoun in 'help him' to refer to the Messenger; al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj prefer this view.
rows.anchor: فعلى هذا تكون الهاء في ينصره للرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو قول ابن عباس والكلبي ومقاتل

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj prefer the pronoun to refer to Muhammad: God aids him in this life by exalting His religion and in the next by raising his rank and avenging his deniers.
rows.anchor: واختاره الفراء والزجاج فالمعنى أن لن ينصر الله محمدا في الدنيا بإعلاء كلمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubters may be Muslims angered at polytheists and impatient for promised victory, or Bedouins who delayed conversion until the Prophet's triumph appeared.
rows.anchor: وظان ذلك قوم من المسلمين لشدة غيظهم على المشركين

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes the pronoun to refer to the person himself, its nearest antecedent: the person fears God will not provide for him and may leave Muhammad's religion.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في ينصره عائد على من لأنه المذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the provision interpretation, naṣara can mean provide, as in the expression 'a rained-on land' and in cited usage of 'help' for giving; even severe frustration cannot change one's allotted provision.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى من كان يظن أن لن يرزقه الله فيعدل عن دين محمد لهذا الظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may instead retain its ordinary sense of victory: an angry person should try every stratagem to secure it and see whether his contrivance removes the frustrating delay.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل على هذا القول أن يكون النصر على بابه أي من كان يظن أن لن ينصره الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an ellipsis: God aids His Messenger, so an envious opponent should exhaust every effort, even self-strangling, to see whether that can undo God's aid.
rows.anchor: أن الله ناصر رسوله في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The strangling is called cutting because it stops breath, and the action is called a plot sarcastically: the plot harms its maker, not the one envied.
rows.anchor: وسمي الاختناق قطعا لأن المختنق يقطع نفسه بحبس مجاريه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the person should stretch a cord toward the covering sky, climb it, and sever the revelation from descending.
rows.anchor: وقيل فليمدد بحبل إلى السماء المظلة وليصعد عليه فليقطع الوحي أن ينزل عليه وهذا قول ابن زيد

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the clearest reading is a proverb: familiar divine victory, cutting by strangling, and sky as the height or roof of air, a tree, or similar place.
rows.anchor: وأبين وجوه هذه الآية أن يكون مثلا ويكون النصر المعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 'what angers him,' ma may be relative, with an omitted antecedent, or a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وما في ما يغيظ بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran was sent down as clear signs, and God creates guidance in the heart of whoever He wills; He alone creates guidance.
rows.anchor: أي ومثل ذلك الإنزال أنزلناه القرآن كله آيات بينات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied antecedent of the pronoun in 'sent it down' is the Quran, understood from context.
rows.anchor: والهاء في أنزلناه للقرآن أضمر للدلالة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance clause means that God creates guidance in the heart of the person He wills to guide; He alone creates guidance.
rows.anchor: والتقدير والأمر أن الله يهدي من يريد أي يخلق الهداية في قلبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage explains whom God guides and leaves unguided, since saying He guides whom He wills entails that He does not guide whom He does not will to guide.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر قبل أن الله يهدي من يريد عقب ببيان من يهديه ومن لا يهديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who associate partners with God include idol worshippers and anyone worshipping something other than God.
rows.anchor: والذين أشركوا هم عبدة الأوثان والأصنام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says إن is repeated in both clauses for emphasis, comparing Jarir's verse; al-Zajjaj makes the same comparison.
rows.anchor: ودخلت إن على كل واحد جزأي الجملة لزيادة التأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poetic comparison is not decisive: Jarir's first clause may be parenthetical, whereas the Quran repeats إن after a long coordinated subject to introduce the predicate.
rows.anchor: ولا يتعين أن يكون البيت كالآية لأن البيت يحتمل أن يكون خبر إن الخليفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The separation on Judgment Day apparently sends believers to Paradise and disbelievers to Hell; ending with 'witness' suits this separation.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الفصل بينهم يوم القيامة هو بصيرورة المؤمنين إلى الجنة والكافرين إلى النار

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the separation broadly as distinction in condition and place: they receive different degrees of recompense and are not gathered in one place.
rows.anchor: الفصل مطلق يحتمل الفصل بينهم في الأحوال والأماكن جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says God judges between believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقيل يفصل بينهم يقضي بين المؤمنين والكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prostration here means willing submission to God's will, embracing rational and nonrational beings and both worshipful and non-ritual submission.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن السجود هنا عبارة عن طواعية ما ذكر تعالى والانقياد لما يريده تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The listed heavenly objects include worshipped angels, the sun worshipped by Himyar, the moon by Kinana, and stars attributed to various Arab tribes; earthly referents include humans, idols, trees, and animals.
rows.anchor: والشمس عبدتها حمير. وعبد القمر كنانة

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri reads al-dawābb with a light bā; Abu al-Fadl says this avoids the geminate, as in other lightened doubled forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري والدواب بتخفيف الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mention of many people does not conflict with all in the earth prostrating: it can refer specifically to worship prostration, or be separately predicated of people rewarded, with other grammatical analyses also possible.
rows.anchor: ولا تعارض بين قوله ومن في الأرض لعمومه وبين قوله وكثير من الناس لخصوصه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses 'many people' as the true people, the righteous and Godfearing, or as a second many upon whom punishment is due; Abū Hayyan calls both analyses weak.
rows.anchor: من الناس خبرا له أي من الناس الذين هم الناس على الحقيقة

rows.speaker: جناح بن حبيش
rows.claim: Janah ibn Hubaysh reads 'and many, great punishment is due to him' with bāʾ instead of thāʾ in kathīr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جناح بن حبيش وكبير حق بالباء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya allows the second 'many' to be coordinated with the earlier list: they prostrate under compulsion through their shadow or when hardship makes them submit; Mujahid likewise says their shadow prostrates.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية وكثير حق عليه العذاب يحتمل أن يكون معطوفا على ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings include kathīran with an accusative cognate, and ḥaqq with a ḍamma on the initial consonant.
rows.anchor: وقرىء وكثير حقا أي حق عليهم العذاب حقا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read mukrim as an active participle, while Ibn Abi Abla reads it as a verbal noun meaning honor or honoring.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور من مكرم اسم فاعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says God humiliates whom He wills through decreed misery, while willing honor or humiliation corresponds to people's deeds and beliefs.
rows.anchor: ومن أهانه الله كتب عليه الشقاوة لما سبق في علمه من كفره أو فسقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan detects Mu'tazili doctrine embedded in al-Zamakhshari's explanation.
rows.anchor: وفيه دسيسة الاعتزال

rows.speaker: قيس بن عباد وهلال بن يساف
rows.claim: They report that the two disputing parties were the champions at Badr: Hamza, Ali, and Ubayda ibn al-Harith against Utba, Shayba, and al-Walid.
rows.anchor: نزلت في المتبارزين يوم بدر حمزة وعلي وعبيدة

rows.speaker: علي وأبو ذر
rows.claim: Ali said he would be the first to kneel for judgment before God on Resurrection Day, and Abu Dharr swore that the verse concerned them; al-Bukhari reports it concerns them.
rows.anchor: أنا أول من يجثو يوم القيامة للخصومة بين يدي الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the disputants were believers and People of the Book, as Jews claimed their religion preceded the believers' faith.
rows.anchor: الإشارة إلى المؤمنين وأهل الكتاب وقع بينهم تخاصم

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعطاء بن أبي رباح والحسن وعاصم والكلبي
rows.claim: These authorities take the two parties as believers and unbelievers generally.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وعطاء بن أبي رباح والحسن وعاصم والكلبي الإشارة إلى المؤمنين والكفار على العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khaṣm is grammatically singular but means a party, so the plural verb follows the individuals within each side; the dispute is over God's religion.
rows.anchor: وخصم مصدر وأريد به هنا الفريق

rows.speaker: الكسائي وابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i transmits khismān with kasra on khāʾ; Ibn Abi Abla reads ikhtaṣamā, preserving dual agreement with the noun.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية عن الكسائي خصمان بكسر الخاء

rows.speaker: الزعفراني
rows.claim: Al-Za'farani reads quṭiʿat with a light ṭāʾ, as if fire makes garments sized to enclose their bodies; the apparent reading means garments of fire.
rows.anchor: قطعت بتخفيف الطاء كأنه تعالى يقدر لهم نيرانا على مقادير جثثهم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the garments are molten copper, heated more intensely than anything else.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير ثياب من نحاس مذاب وليس شيء إذا حمي أشد حرارة منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation treats fire garments as a metaphor for the fire enveloping them as clothes envelop their wearers.
rows.anchor: الثياب من النار استعارة عن إحاطة النار بهم

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says Hell's inhabitants are clothed, though nakedness would be better for them, and kept alive, though death would be better.
rows.anchor: يكسى أهل النار والعري خير لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a single drop of the boiling liquid would melt the world's mountains.
rows.anchor: لو سقطت من الحميم نقطة على جبال الدنيا لأذابتها

rows.speaker: الحسن وفرقة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and a group read yaṣharu with an open ṣād and doubled hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وفرقة يصهر بفتح الصاد وتشديد الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse describes boiling liquid melting the innards and reaching the outer skin, affecting it as it does the interior; another verse similarly says it cuts their bowels.
rows.anchor: وما يصب على الرأس ذكر ما يصل إلى باطن المعذب وهو الحميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophetic report says boiling liquid passes through the skull and entrails and exits through the feet, after which the victim is restored as before.
rows.anchor: إن الحميم ليصب على رؤوسهم فينفذ الجمجمة حتى يخلص إلى جوفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apparently 'and the skins' coordinates with 'what is in their bellies,' so skins melt too; another parse supplies 'pierce' because skin is not melted but contracts on fire, like an omitted verb in a cited poem.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عطف والجلود على ما من قوله يصهر به ما في بطونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'and for them' refers to unbelievers and the lam marks entitlement; it may mean 'upon' or refer contextually to the guards.
rows.anchor: عائد على الكفار، واللام للاستحقاق

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and others explain the iron maqaamiʿ as hammers; another view calls them whips of fire.
rows.anchor: المقامع المطارق. وقيل: سياط من نار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says that if one of the iron clubs were placed on earth, all people and jinn together could not lift it.
rows.anchor: «لو وضع مقمع منها في الأرض ثم اجتمع عليه الثقلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min gham is parsed as an inclusive genitive substitute with the preposition repeated and its pronoun omitted; alternatively, min marks the cause of their grief.
rows.anchor: من غم بدل من منها بدل اشتمال، أعيد معه الجار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return is apparently tied to wanting to escape, with an implied reference to their prepared places of torment; another view says guards strike them back and tell them to taste the punishment.
rows.anchor: والظاهر تعليق الإعادة على الإرادة للخروج فلا بد من محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After describing the punishment prepared for one disputing party, the passage turns to the reward prepared for the other.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى ما أعد لأحد الخصمين من العذاب

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read yuḥallawna with a doubled lām; another reading lightens it, while Ibn Abbas reads the active form yaḥlawna.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور يحلون بضم الياء وفتح الحاء وتشديد اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu al-Fadl's derivation of yaḥlawna from 'to please the eye' wrongly makes the verb transitive and min extra; Abu Hayyan instead explains min causally or as a substitute for bi.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بجيد لأنه جعل حلي فعلا متعديا ولذلك حكم بزيادة من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in 'bracelets' apparently marks partitive selection, while min in 'gold' marks the material from which they are made.
rows.anchor: والظاهر إن من في من أساور للتبعيض وفي من ذهب لابتداء الغاية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya allows min in 'bracelets' to explain the kind, or alternatively to indicate a part.
rows.anchor: من في من أساور لبيان الجنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads aswar without alif or hāʾ, with fatḥa on the final rāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس من أسور بفتح الراء من غير ألف ولا هاء

rows.speaker: عاصم ونافع والحسن والجحدري والأعرج وأبو جعفر وعيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: These readers use the accusative lu'lu'an; Abu al-Fath supplies an omitted verb meaning 'they are given pearls,' while other analyses coordinate it with the grammatical position of bracelets.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم ونافع والحسن والجحدري والأعرج وأبو جعفر وعيسى بن عمر

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة والحسن وطلحة وابن وثاب والأعمش وأهل مكة
rows.claim: These readers use the genitive lu'lu'in, coordinating it with bracelets or gold since bracelets may be made from both.
rows.anchor: وأهل مكة ولؤلؤ بالخفض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present verb may express continuing action, refer back to the past in coordination with 'disbelieved,' or have an implied subject; proposed predicates for inn differ, with al-Zamakhshari's reading best supported by the following conditional clause.
rows.anchor: المضارع قد لا يلحظ فيه زمان معين من حال أو استقبال فيدل إذ ذاك على الاستمرار

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya proposes an omitted predicate after 'the resident and the visitor' meaning they have lost or perished.
rows.anchor: وخبر إن محذوف قدره ابن عطية بعد والباد خسروا أو هلكوا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari places the omitted predicate after 'the Sacred Mosque' and supplies God's threat of painful punishment; Abu Hayyan prefers this because the conditional clause supports it lexically.
rows.anchor: وقدره الزمخشري بعد قوله الحرام نذيقهم من عذاب أليم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects the proposal that the waw is extra and 'they bar' itself is the predicate of inn, because that corrupts the intended sense; Basrans reject extra waw.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا مفسد للمعنى المقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was revealed at Hudaybiyya when the Prophet was prevented from the Sacred Mosque; no earlier mass exclusion is known, though individuals may have been barred early in the mission.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية نزلت عام الحديبية حين صد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning is the Mosque itself; another view means the entire sanctuary, since the Prophet and his companions were expelled from it, though the Mosque is the main focus.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه نفس المسجد ومن صد عن الوصول إليه فقد صد عنه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read sawāʾ in the nominative, taking the clause as a second object of 'made'; most naturally the resident and visitor are subject and 'equal' predicate, though the reverse is possible.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور سواء بالرفع على أن الجملة من مبتدأ وخبر في موضع المفعول الثاني

rows.speaker: حفص والأعمش
rows.claim: Hafs and al-A'mash read sawāʾ in the accusative, governed as a verbal noun meaning 'equal'; it is either the second object of jaʿala or a circumstantial expression.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص والأعمش سواء بالنصب وارتفع به العاكف لأنه مصدر في معنى مستو

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: A further al-A'mash reading has accusative sawāʾ and genitive al-ākif; Ibn Atiyya calls the latter apposition to 'people,' while Abu Hayyan prefers a specifying substitute.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة منهم الأعمش في رواية القطعي سواء بالنصب العاكف فيه بالجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three forms of the alif in al-bādi are reported: retained in both connected and paused reading, omitted in both, or retained in connection but omitted at pause.
rows.anchor: وقرىء والبادي وصلا ووقفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ākif means a resident; al-bādi means a newcomer.
rows.anchor: العاكف المقيم فيه والبادي الطارئ عليه

rows.speaker: عمر وابن عباس ومجاهد وجماعة
rows.claim: All agree that access is equal within the Sacred Mosque, but these authorities extend the rule to Mecca: a visitor may lodge anywhere and the owner must host him; al-Thawri agrees, as was early practice.
rows.anchor: فذهب عمر وابن عباس ومجاهد وجماعة

rows.speaker: ابن سابط
rows.claim: Ibn Sabit says Meccan houses initially had no doors; Umar objected when a resident shut his door against pilgrims, then accepted the need to protect goods from theft, after which people installed doors.
rows.anchor: وكانت دورهم بغير أبواب حتى كثرت السرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute over visitors' access to houses follows a legal dispute about whether Mecca was conquered by force or treaty.
rows.anchor: وهذا الخلاف مترتب على الخلاف في فتح مكة أكان عنوة أو صلحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilḥād means deviation from the right course; the author prefers construing yurīd as 'be involved in,' which governs the preposition bi, so the threat covers any wrongdoing rather than listed examples alone.
rows.anchor: والإلحاد الميل عن القصد. ومفعول برد

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda calls the preposition in bi-ilḥād extra in the object position, citing a line by al-A'sha where bi introduces 'provision.'
rows.anchor: هو بإلحاد والباء زائدة في المفعول

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the sense could be that someone intends to bar people there through wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون التقدير ومن يرد فيه الناس بإلحاد

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari treats bi-ilḥād and bi-ẓulm as two circumstantial expressions while leaving the object of 'intends' general, so any wrongful intent is covered.
rows.anchor: بإلحاد بظلم حالان مترادفتان ومفعول يرد متروك

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies wrongdoing in the sanctuary as hoarding.
rows.anchor: وعن سعيد بن جبير: الاحتكار

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata identifies it as a trader's unnecessary swearing, saying 'no, by God' and 'yes, by God.'
rows.anchor: وعن عطاء: قول الرجل في المبايعة لا والله وبلى والله

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says even intending an evil deed without doing it is accountable in Mecca.
rows.anchor: فلو نوى سيئة ولم يعملها لم يحاسب بها إلا في مكة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains ilḥād as associating partners with God, and elsewhere as declaring the forbidden lawful.
rows.anchor: الإلحاد هنا الشرك. وقال أيضا: هو استحلال الحرام

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says ilḥād is any bad deed in the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هو العمل السيء فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar includes the words 'no, by God' and 'yes, by God' among forms of ilḥād.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عمر: لا والله وبلى والله من الإلحاد

rows.speaker: حبيب بن أبي ثابت
rows.claim: Habib ibn Abi Thabit says hoarding in Mecca counts as wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: وقال حبيب بن أبي ثابت: الحكر بمكة من الإلحاد بالظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan treats these reports as examples, not exhaustive definitions, because the wording itself is general.
rows.anchor: والأولى حمل هذه الأقوال على التمثيل لا على الحصر إذ الكلام يدل على العموم

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' report an open-yā reading of yurīd, from warada, meaning whoever comes to the sanctuary while acting wrongfully.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة ومن يرد بفتح الياء من الورود وحكاها الكسائي والفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After condemning the disbelievers' exclusion from the Mosque and their wrongdoing there, the passage recalls their ancestor Abraham and reproaches their idol worship.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى حال الكفار وصدهم عن المسجد الحرام وتوعد فيه من أراد فيه بإلحاد ذكر حال أبيهم إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh bawwa'na means 'remember when We assigned Abraham the location of the House,' a place to which people return for construction and worship.
rows.anchor: وإذ بوأنا أي واذكر إذ بوأنا أي جعلنا لإبراهيم مكان البيت مباءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternative syntax makes the lam extra, or supplies 'people' as the object and takes the lam as causal, meaning God assigned the place for Abraham's honor and through him.
rows.anchor: تقديره بوأنا الناس، واللام في لإبراهيم لام العلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to associate partners and the following commands apparently address Abraham; another view addresses Muhammad and treats an as a reduced particle, but Abu Hayyan prefers the subjunctive complement because bawwa'na is not a speech verb.
rows.anchor: والأولى عندي أن تكون أن الناصبة للمضارع إذ يليها الفعل المتصرف

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains that the location was assigned for worship, so the command to Abraham not to associate partners and to purify the House explains its purpose.
rows.anchor: كانت التبوئة مقصودة من أجل العبادة

rows.speaker: عكرمة وأبو نهيك
rows.claim: Ikrima and Abu Nuhaik read 'that he not associate' in the third person, reporting what Abraham was commanded; Abu Hatim requires the kāf to be accusative on this reading.
rows.anchor: أن لا يشرك بالياء على معنى أن يقول معنى القول الذي قيل له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The 'ones standing' refers to those praying, naming standing, bowing, and prostration as the greatest pillars of prayer.
rows.anchor: والقائمون هم المصلون ذكر من أركانها أعظمها وهو القيام والركوع والسجود

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read wa-adhdhin with a doubled dhāl, meaning 'proclaim'; a report says Abraham ascended Abu Qubays and called people to pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور وأذن بالتشديد أي ناد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the address is to the Prophet, who was commanded to make the proclamation during the Farewell Pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وتقدم قول من قال إنه خطاب للرسول

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin read ādhana with a long vowel and light dhāl; Abu Hayyan rejects Ibn Atiyya's claim that this report was a scribal error and cites Ibn Khallawayh and al-Lawāmiʿ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن محيصن وآذن بمدة وتخفيف الذال

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الرازي
rows.claim: Abu al-Fadl says the long-vowel reading coordinates with 'when We assigned,' with the order advanced and delayed, and 'they will come' is jussive as the response to 'purify.'
rows.anchor: ويصير يأتوك جزما على جواب الأمر الذي هو وطهر

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Ishaq reads al-ḥajj with a kasra on ḥāʾ wherever it occurs; the majority use a fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي إسحاق بالحج بكسر الحاء حيث وقع الجمهور بفتحها

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق وعكرمة والحسن وأبو مجلز
rows.claim: These authorities read rijālan with ḍamma on rāʾ and a light jīm, a collective noun like zu'ār; a doubled jīm is also transmitted from them and other authorities.
rows.anchor: وابن أبي إسحاق بضم الراء والتخفيف

rows.speaker: عكرمة وابن عباس وعطاء وابن حدير
rows.claim: Other readings include rijālī with a final alif maqṣūra, with a doubled jīm in some transmissions; rijāl is also a plural of rājil, as tujjār is of tājir.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة أيضا رجالى على وزن النعامى بألف التأنيث المقصورة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read ya'tīna, with the pronoun referring to each lean camel since distant routes to Mecca are normally traveled mounted; it may figuratively include men and beasts as caravans.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور يأتين فالظاهر عود الضمير على كل ضامر

rows.speaker: عبد الله وأصحابه والضحاك وابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: These readers use masculine ya'tūn, prioritizing the rational masculine antecedent; Ibn Abbas regretted not having made pilgrimage on foot.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وأصحابه والضحاك وابن أبي عبلة يأتون غلب العقلاء الذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is weak to infer that pilgrimage is not obligatory for someone whose only route is by sea because the verse omits ships: Mecca is not on a sea, and it names the means of reaching it.
rows.anchor: لأن مكة ليست على بحر، وإنما يتوصل إليها

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reads fajj 'amīq as fajj maʿīq, a distant route.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود فج معيق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and others explain the pilgrimage benefits as trade; al-Baqir says they mean reward, and Mujahid and Ata include both senses, a view chosen by Ibn al-Arabi.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وعطاء كلاهما، واختاره ابن العربي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the indefinite 'benefits' signals distinctive spiritual and worldly benefits of pilgrimage absent from other worship; Abu Hanifa ranked Hajj first after witnessing them.
rows.anchor: ونكر المنافع لأنه أراد منافع مختصة بهذه العبادة دينية ودنياوية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Mentioning God's name is a metonym for sacrifice, since Muslims name God when sacrificing; the phrasing emphasizes that God's remembrance is the primary purpose and is rhetorically superior to simply saying 'slaughter.'
rows.anchor: وكنى عن النحر والذبح بذكر اسم الله لأن أهل الإسلام لا ينفكون عن ذكر اسمه

rows.speaker: مالك وأصحاب الرأي
rows.claim: They infer that slaughter at night is impermissible because sacrifice is restricted to 'days.'
rows.anchor: واستدل من قال أن المقصود بذكر اسم الله هو على الذبح والنحر على أن الذبح لا يكون بالليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes remembrance as praising and sanctifying God in gratitude for provision, supported by a prophetic statement that these are days of eating and drinking.
rows.anchor: الذكر هنا حمده وتقديسه شكرا على نعمته في الرزق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وإبراهيم وقتادة وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: They identify the 'known days' as the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijja and the 'numbered days' as the three days of Tashriq.
rows.anchor: وذكر اسم الله والأيام المعلومات أيام العشر قاله ابن عباس والحسن وإبراهيم وقتادة وأبو حنيفة

rows.speaker: مالك وأصحابه
rows.claim: They define the known days as the day of sacrifice and the next two, and the numbered days as all three Tashriq days, so the fourth is numbered but not known.
rows.anchor: المعلومات يوم النحر ويومان بعده

rows.speaker: علي وابن عباس وابن عمر وأنس وأبو هريرة وسعيد بن جبير وسعيد بن المسيب وأبو حنيفة والثوري
rows.claim: These authorities allow sacrifice on the day of sacrifice and the following two; Hasan, Ata, and al-Shafi'i allow three days after it, al-Nakha'i two days, Ibn Sirin one day, and Abu Salama and Sulayman ibn Yasar until Muharram's new moon.
rows.anchor: ويوم النحر ويومان بعده هي أيام النحر عند علي وابن عباس وابن عمر وأنس وأبي هريرة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya suggests both day descriptions may cover all the virtuous days; their purpose is to urge people to seize the special opportunity rather than delimit slaughter or hastening.
rows.anchor: ويظهر أن تكون المعلومات والمعدودات بمعنى أن تلك الأيام الفاضلة كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bahīmat al-anʿām specifies the otherwise broad term bahīmah: camels, cattle, sheep, and goats; an earlier discussion in al-Ma'ida treated its scope.
rows.anchor: والبهيمة مبهمة في كل ذات أربع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent rule makes eating sacrificial meat and feeding the poor obligatory; other views recommend both, or recommend eating while requiring feeding.
rows.anchor: والظاهر وجوب الأكل والإطعام. وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bā'is is someone struck by hardship.
rows.anchor: والبائس الذي أصابه بؤس أي شدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafath comprises acts at release from ihram, such as trimming or shaving hair and removing dishevelment, after completion of the rites; Ibn Umar says it means the obligations or all rites of Hajj.
rows.anchor: ما يصنعه المحرم عند حله من تقصير شعر وحلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vows are charitable acts pilgrims vow to perform; alternatively, the phrase means fulfilling what is obligatory whether vowed or not.
rows.anchor: والنذور هنا ما ينذرونه من أعمال البر في حجهم

rows.speaker: شعبة عن عاصم والجمهور
rows.claim: Shu'ba from Asim reads li-yuwaffū with a doubled fāʾ; the majority read it lightly.
rows.anchor: وقرأ شعبة عن عاصم وليوفوا مشددا والجمهور مخففا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority identify the commanded circumambulation as ṭawāf al-ifāḍa, the visitation circumambulation, a pillar of Hajj that completes release from ihram; another view calls it the farewell circumambulation.
rows.anchor: وليطوفوا هو طواف الإفاضة وهو طواف الزيارة الذي هو من أركان الحج

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says interpreters agree that the circumambulation is ṭawāf al-ifāḍa, while Ibn Atiyya allows the farewell reading based on sequence.
rows.anchor: لا خلاف بين المتأولين أنه طواف الإفاضة

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن زيد
rows.claim: They explain al-ʿatīq as ancient.
rows.anchor: العتيق القديم قاله الحسن وابن زيد

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير وابن أبي نجيح وقتادة
rows.claim: They say the House is protected from tyrants; would-be destroyers such as Tubba' and Abraha were struck down, although al-Hajjaj attacked Ibn al-Zubayr who had taken shelter there.
rows.anchor: أو المعتق من الجبابرة قاله ابن الزبير وابن أبي نجيح وقتادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن جبير
rows.claim: Other explanations say the House was never owned, was freed from the Flood, or is a noble, excellent place; Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr report the flood explanation.
rows.anchor: أو المحرر لم يملك موضعه قط قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also says the House frees the necks of sinners from punishment through visitation and circumambulation; Abu Hayyan rejects Ibn Atiyya's morphological objection, explaining the form as a figurative active meaning 'one that frees.'
rows.anchor: ولا يرده التصريف لأنه فسره تفسير معنى

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya supplies 'your prescribed duty' as the omitted predicate after 'that'; al-Zamakhshari supplies 'the matter,' a transition into a new topic.
rows.anchor: ذلك خبر مبتدأ محذوف قدره ابن عطية فرضكم ذلك أو الواجب ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other analyses make the demonstrative the topic with an omitted predicate or an object meaning 'comply with that'; Zuhayr's verse offers a comparable rhetorical transition.
rows.anchor: وقيل في موضع نصب تقديره امتثلوا ذلك ونظير هذه الإشارة البليغة قول زهير

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The forbidden sanctities may mean the rites commanded in Hajj.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل الخصوص بما يتعلق بالحج وقاله الكلبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the sanctities as all prohibitions of Hajj, including sexual relations, quarrelling, and hunting.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس هي جميع المناهي في الحج

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd counts five sanctities: the sacred waymark, mosque, House, month, and pilgrim in ihram until release.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن زيد هي خمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of sanctities is general: anything God forbids violating, including all religious obligations.
rows.anchor: والحرمات ما لا يحل هتكه وجميع التكليفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'it is better for him' refers to magnifying the sanctities, which earns nearness to God and reward; khayr means good rather than comparative goodness.
rows.anchor: وضمير فهو عائد على المصدر المفهوم من قوله ومن يعظم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permission for livestock responds to pre-Islamic self-imposed bans such as bahīrah and sā'ibah; the exception refers to animals whose prohibition Scripture states.
rows.anchor: وأحلت لكم بهيمة الأنعام دفعا لما كانت عليه من تحريم أشياء برأيها كالبحيرة والسائبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After magnifying God's sanctities, the verse commands avoiding idols and false speech because monotheism and truthfulness are the greatest sanctities; idolatry itself is falsehood.
rows.anchor: ولما حث على تعظيم حرمات الله وذكر أن تعظيمها خير لمعظمها عند الله أتبعه الأمر باجتناب الأوثان وقول الزور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min may specify the kind of impurity as idols, or mark its source, making idol worship the origin of all corruption and impurity; on the first parse, other impurities are prohibited elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ومن في من الأوثان لبيان الجنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وجماعة
rows.claim: They identify God's waymarks here as sacrificial camels and say honoring them means fattening them and taking care over their value.
rows.anchor: هي البدن الهدايا، وتعظيمها تسمينها

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam lists six waymarks, including Safa, Marwa, sacrifices, the pillars, Mash'ar al-Haram, Arafat, and the Corner; honoring them means fulfilling their due rites.
rows.anchor: الشعائر ست: الصفا، والمروة، والبدن، والجمار

rows.speaker: ابن عمر والحسن ومالك وابن زيد
rows.claim: They define the waymarks as all Hajj sites and landmarks, including Mina, Arafat, Muzdalifa, Safa, Marwa, and the House.
rows.anchor: مواضع الحج كلها ومعالمه بمنى وعرفة والمزدلفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the waymarks as religious laws, whose observance benefits people until the end of legal responsibility; 'in them' refers to the laws, and the place where they end is variously identified with the House or its Lord.
rows.anchor: شرائع دينه وتعظيمها التزامها والمنافع الأجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God attaches piety to hearts; a prophetic report points to the chest, since hypocrites display piety outwardly without sincerity while the sincere exert themselves in worship.
rows.anchor: كما قال عليه الصلاة والسلام: «التقوى هاهنا»

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar offered a she-camel valued at three hundred dinars; when he asked whether to sell it for several sacrifices, the Prophet told him to offer that camel itself.
rows.anchor: وعن عمر أنه أهدى نجيبة طلبت منه بثلاثمائة دينار فسأل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet offered one hundred camels, including Abu Jahl's camel with a gold nose ring; Ibn Umar gave the camels' meat and coverings in charity.
rows.anchor: وأهدى هو عليه السلام مائة بدنة فيها جمل لأبي جهل في أنفه برة من ذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning hearts distinguishes sincere worship from hypocritical outward display: sincere piety drives one to perform acts of obedience fully.
rows.anchor: وذكر القلوب لأن المنافق يظهر التقوى وقلبه خال عنها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari understands the phrase as magnifying God's signs being an act of people whose hearts possess piety; the heart is its center, whose settled effect appears in the limbs.
rows.anchor: فإن تعظيمها من أفعال ذوي تقوى القلوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says al-Zamakhshari's ellipsis lacks a pronoun linking the result to the conditional subject; the sentence needs 'from him' to supply that link.
rows.anchor: وما قدره عار من راجع إلى الجزاء إلى من ألا ترى أن قوله فإن تعظيمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with al-qulūb nominative makes hearts the subject of the verbal noun taqwā.
rows.anchor: وقرىء القلوب بالرفع على الفاعلية بالمصدر الذي هو تقوى

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The pronoun in 'in them are benefits' apparently refers to sacrificial animals: milk, offspring, wool, and riding before they are designated and obligated as offerings.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فيها عائد على البدن على قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة والضحاك
rows.claim: They say the deadline ends when the animal is assigned as an offering, after which the owner has no further use of it.
rows.anchor: إلى أجل مسمى وهو أن يسميها ويوجبها هديا فليس له شيء من منافعها

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata permits riding an offering or drinking its milk when needed after it has been assigned, until slaughter.
rows.anchor: منافع الهدايا بعد إيجابها وتسميتها هديا بأن تركب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other deadlines are the animal's marking, departure from Mecca, departure from the waymarks, or Judgment Day; al-Zamakhshari says the benefit ends when it is slaughtered, distributed, and eaten.
rows.anchor: إلى أن تشعر فلا تركب إلا عند الضرورة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the offering's terminal point is slaughter, distribution of its meat, and eating from it.
rows.anchor: إلى أن تنحر ويتصدق بلحومها ويؤكل منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma marks delayed sequence figuratively: offerings have worldly and religious benefits, but the greatest is their endpoint at the House, meaning the duty or time of slaughter in the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وأعظم هذه المنافع وأبعدها شوطا في النفع محلها إلى البيت أي وجوب نحرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mansak may derive from nusuk as a place of worship or a verbal noun, and may mean worship generally, a specific rite, a slaughtering place, or sacrifice itself; al-Zamakhshari chooses slaughter for God with His name invoked.
rows.anchor: والمنسك مفعل من نسك واحتمل أن يكون موضعا للنسك

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read mansak with a fatḥa on the sīn, matching the usual pattern for a verbal noun or place from a verb whose present form has ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وقياس بناء مفعل مما مضارعه يفعل يضم العين مفعل بفتحها في المصدر والزمان والمكان

rows.speaker: الأخوان وابن سعدان وأبو حاتم عن أبي عمرو ويونس ومحبوب وعبد الوارث
rows.claim: These readers use a kasra; Ibn Atiyya calls it anomalous and nonproductive, perhaps learned by al-Kisa'i from Arabs, while al-Azhari accepts both forms as dialectal variants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بكسرها الأخوان وابن سعدان وأبو حاتم عن أبي عمرو ويونس ومحبوب وعبد الوارث

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid defines mansak as slaughtering and spilling blood, noting that nasaka means slaughter and nasīkah is a sacrificial animal.
rows.anchor: المنسك الذبح، وإراقة الدماء يقال: نسك إذا ذبح

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra' explains mansak as a customary practice of goodness and charity, and elsewhere as a festival.
rows.anchor: المنسك في كلام العرب المعتاد في خير وبر

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn Arafa glosses it as a path of obedience to God: one follows the practice of a people by adopting their way.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عرفة منسكا أي مذهبا من طاعة الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies mansak with pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء منسكا عيدا وقال قتادة: حجا

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says a voluntary offering that becomes incapacitated before reaching Mecca is slaughtered where it falls; if it reaches Mina, the place of slaughter is anywhere within Mecca's routes.
rows.anchor: وقال القفال: الهدي المتطوع به إذا عطب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says thumma orders clauses rather than time; for the reported views, the place is the slaughter site and the deadline is returning for ṭawāf al-ifāḍa, so the House is meant literally, as Malik says in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: وتكرر ثم لترتيب الجمل

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن عمر وابن عيسى
rows.claim: Mujahid says the sacrificial camels are tethered; Ibn Umar says they stand aligned with their forelegs tied, and Ibn Isa says they are lined up.
rows.anchor: معقولة. وقال ابن عمر: قائمة قد صفت أيديها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God's name at slaughter means saying 'God is greatest; there is no god but God; God is greatest; from You and to You.'
rows.anchor: وذكر اسم الله أن يقول عند النحر الله أكبر لا إله إلا الله والله أكبر

rows.speaker: أبو موسى الأشعري والحسن ومجاهد وزيد بن أسلم وشقيق وسليمان التيمي والأعرج
rows.claim: These readers read ṣawāfī, meaning offerings reserved purely for God; Amr ibn Ubayd marks the ending with tanwīn. Al-Zamakhshari treats tanwīn as compensating for a dropped letter at pause, while Abu Hayyan favors declension of an otherwise indeclinable form.
rows.anchor: صوافي جمع صافية ونون الياء عمرو بن عبيد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also reads ṣawāff, understood like an adjective meaning bare or uncovered.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن أيضا صواف مثل عوار

rows.speaker: عبد الله وابن عمر وابن عباس والباقر وقتادة ومجاهد وعطاء والضحاك والكلبي والأعمش
rows.claim: These authorities read ṣawāfin with nūn; a ṣāfinah is an animal balanced on a hoof, a description more commonly used of horses.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وابن عمر وابن عباس والباقر وقتادة ومجاهد وعطاء والضحاك والكلبي والأعمش بخلاف عنه صوافن بالنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the animals' sides fall, it means they have collapsed to the ground after slaughter.
rows.anchor: فإذا وجبت جنوبها عبارة عن سقوطها إلى الأرض بعد نحرها

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب ومجاهد وإبراهيم والحسن والكلبي
rows.claim: They define al-qāniʿ as a beggar and al-mu'tarr as someone who comes without asking; another group reverses these definitions.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن كعب ومجاهد وإبراهيم والحسن والكلبي القانع السائل والمعتر المعترض من غير سؤال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports two explanations from Ibn Abbas: the qāniʿ is content with what he receives and the mu'tarr comes without asking; another transmission calls the qāniʿ self-restrained and the mu'tarr a beggar.
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري عن ابن عباس القانع المستغني بما أعطيه والمعتر المعترض من غير سؤال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the qāniʿ is a neighbor, even if wealthy.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد القانع الجار وإن كان غنيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada derives qāniʿ from contentment and makes the mu'tarr one who approaches seeking help; another view calls the latter a visiting friend.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة القانع من القناعة والمعتر المعترض للسؤال

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء
rows.claim: Abu Raja reads al-qanaʿ without the alif, with the alif omitted as in similar shortened forms; other variant reports read al-mu'tari or al-mu'tar without yāʾ.
rows.anchor: القنع بغير ألف أي القانع فحذف الألف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains al-mu'tar as al-mu'tarr with its yāʾ omitted for lightness and the kasra serving in its place; the same is transmitted from Abu Raja.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس برواية المقري والمعتر أراد المعتري لكنه حذف الياء تخفيفا
